NHL may not be a household name, but its all-new, all-electric NTE240E ultra-class haul track could change that with a 240 ton payload, over 4.1 MWh of battery, advanced regenerative braking, and a world’s first double-gun MCS charging setup.
For the uninitiated, Inner Mongolia North Hauler Joint Stock Co., Ltd. (NHL) is a Chinese heavy equipment manufacturer specializing in the enormous rigid-frame haul trucks used in open-pit mining operations. Established in 1988, NHL has decades of experience building mining trucks for customers around the world, including some of the industry’s largest diesel-electric hybrids. The brand’s new NTE240E is different, representing a company’s real push into battery-electric mining equipment, and it’s powering that push with some seriously ambitious technology.
Let’s start with the battery. The NTE240E packs an absolutely MASSIVE battery pack, with the highest-capacity versions offering up to 4,100 kWh (4.1 MWh) of onboard energy storage. Keeping that much battery topped off is no small task, which is why NHL developed an equally ambitious energy replenishment strategy supporting dual-gun MCS charging, allowing its town-sized battery to go from 20% to 90% in under an hour.
That means operators can take advantage of shift changes and scheduled rest breaks to top off the battery without sacrificing an entire work shift to charging – but even more impressive than the fact that all that juice can be crammed into so big a battery in so little time is the fact that, according to NHL, it can be done at just 25°C (about 77°F).

More than way to power up
Plugging in isn’t the only way the NTE240E drinks its juice. NHL’s new dynamic power reception system uses overhead current collectors to supply electricity directly to the truck while it’s climbing loaded mine roads , allowing it to then “ ride the brakes ” for more energy all the way downhill.
The combined technologies allow NHL’s operators to keep the massive trucks moving without relying entirely on their onboard batteries. The result is a claimed 15% improvement in energy efficiency over the ultra-class industry average.
That efficiency turns into savings, which means the economics of running an NTE240E could be just as compelling as the emissions savings – and those are substantial . NHL says each NTE240E can reduce harmful carbon emissions by more than 2,000 tons annually, even as it cuts operating costs by more than 60% compared to a comparably capable diesel.
What’s more, because the big BEV’s electrical system eliminates the need for engine-related hardware like generators and the maintenance and overhaul costs associated with those components. Taken as a whole, the NHL seems to be a compelling offering … but that’s not for me to say. You guys are the experts – let us know what you think of the new NHL NTE240E, in the comments.

The UK's Renault Twingo EV Retails From £14,745 After Full £3,750 Electric Car Grant
169 photos
Photo: Renault
Renault has managed to price its cutesy Twingo E-Tech from £14,745 in the United Kingdom, and the French automaker hasn't achieved that figure by ripping out features that come in handy on a daily basis. A proper automobile instead of a glorified mobility scooter, the small hatch can be this affordable by folding the £3,750 electric vehicle grant into the advertised price.
Remove it, and the base Evolution grade would otherwise cost £18,495 before optional extras. A decidedly less interesting number, for sure. In the United Kingdom, the Twingo E-Tech gets a front-mounted electric drive unit with close to 80 ponies to its name, along with a 27.5-kWh battery.
A lithium-iron-phosphate battery, that is, for the nickel-manganese-cobalt alternative would be too expensive for a low-cost vehicle. In the WLTP, the French automaker's British division expects no more than 163 miles (262 kilometers) of driving on a full charge of said LFP battery.
Measuring just under 3.8 meters, which is nearly 150 inches over in the United States (where Renault packed up and left in 1987), the zero-emission hatchback measures 2,493 millimeters (98.1 inches) between its front and rear axles. Not bad for such a small vehicle, especially when you remember that Ford's discontinued Fiesta used to measure 2,493 millimeters in wheelbase as well.
Gifted with playful styling and perfectly so proportions, the retro-tastic hatchback won't be mistaken for any other cheap battery-electric vehicle on the road. Its cheerful personality carries over inside, where four occupants can squeeze in. The rear seats can be folded independently, and they also slide for good measure.
Photo: Renault Both solutions allow the driver to strike a balance between passenger and cargo space without sacrificing the entire back row, and this versatility is exactly what you'd expect from a small European hatchback. The Renault UK configurator lists anything from 305 liters at minimum and up to 1,010 liters (35.7 cubic feet) tops with the rear seats folded and slid in the most cargo-favoring position.
Rated at 175 Newton-meters (just under 130 pound-feet) of twist, the Twingo E-Tech needs a leisurely 12.1 seconds to hit 62 miles per hour (100 kilometers per hour). Top speed? An honest 130 kilometers per hour (nearly 81 miles per hour), which means that highway driving at Europe's posted top speeds of 70 mph in the UK and 130 kph in many continental regions would max it out.
Charging, however, is a compromise of sorts. Renault may have included an 11-kW AC charger, but fast charging on DC tops 50 kilowatts. The battery's capacity negates the poor DC performance, though. In optimal conditions, you need half an hour to recharge the LFP battery pack from 10 to 80 percent.
Evolution customers get 16-inch steel wheels by default, along with decorative covers for them, a 7-inch display for the driver, 10-inch touchscreen infotainment, manual air conditioning, cruise control, lane-keeping assist, rear parking sensors, traffic sign recognition, and automatic emergency braking. The better-equipped Techno adds larger alloys, automatic climate control, a reversing camera, heated front seats, Google built-in services, one-pedal driving, and a hands-free key card.
Stepping up to the Launch Edition, prospective customers are presented with rear cross-traffic alert, hands-free parking, blind-spot warning, an interior equipment pack, and free-of-charge paint options. Those would be Mango Yellow and Absolute Green, the latter being my favorite shade available this model year.

© Iakov Filimonov
By Gavin van Marle
20 November 2026
Container spot freight rates on the transpacific trades finally began to show more normal slack-season behaviour this week, with significant declines from Asia to both the US west and east coasts.
However, spot rates on the Asia-Europe trade moved in the opposite direction, with Asia-Mediterranean rates showing a small spike after three weeks of flatlining.
This week’s World Container Index (WCI) from Drewry recorded spot rates on its Shanghai-Genoa leg up 6% over the previous seven days, to finish at $4,436 per 40ft, while Shanghai-Rotterdam was unchanged, at $3,496 per 40ft.
European forwarders expressed some surprise at the strength of the Asia-Mediterranean pricing, which appeared slightly divorced from demand and supply fundamentals.
“Yes, we did see a big hike mid-November on rates for Asia to Med, but we’ve not seen a big jump in demand, or issues with getting space, so it’s a bit of a head-scratcher, especially with more Med services going through Suez now,” one told The Loadstar .
He added that further hikes had been notified for the first half of December, through a mixture of new FAK levels – broadly in the range of $4,500 per 40ft to North Europe and $5,500 to the Med – as well as pre-Chinese New Year peak season surcharges (PSS), currently ranging from $1,000-$1,600 per 40ft, depending on carrier and destination, due to be implemented on 1 December.
“It depends on the carrier, but we are seeing a mix of base rate increases and surcharge add-ons, and we’re seeing the same for North Europe for the first half of December.
“But the rate increase doesn’t seem to match demand levels, so we are not sure it will all stick. It’s also quite early to get December levels, so it feels like a punt from the carriers at this stage,” he added.
On the Transpacific, rates continued their downward trend on the WCI, for the seventh consecutive week, Drewry noted, its Shanghai-New York rate declining 9% week on week, to finish at $8,194 per 40ft, while the Shanghai-Los Angeles leg was down 5%, to $7,026 per 40ft.
Today’s levels are the lowest Asia-US east coast spot rates in 15 weeks, and the lowest to the west coast for 12 weeks.
According to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, 10 blank sailings have been announced for next week, compared with four this week, although the analyst said that, “despite these capacity reductions, Drewry expects freight rates to decrease further next week”.
However, US west coast forwarder Freight Right warned shippers that steep pricing falls were unlikely in the short term.
“Looking ahead to the remainder of November and early December, ocean freight rates are expected to remain largely stable,” it said.
“Importers should not anticipate dramatic rate drops, as carriers are strategically maintaining baseline pricing in preparation for the January shipping cycle.
“However, because carriers still have scheduled weekly sailings, and want to avoid moving empty vessels, shippers may see targeted, vessel-specific promotional rates emerge in early December,” it added.
However, there is also more capacity entering the trade over the next two-to-three weeks.
Zim is set to launch a new premium transpacific liner service between China and the US on 5 December. The ZX3 will deploy five ships with an average capacity of 4,300 teu on a Xiamen-Shanghai-Los Angeles rotation, with a 12-day transit time.
Meanwhile, MSC notified shippers today it would reinstate its transpacific Mustang service from Asia to the Pacific north-west coast, which it suspended at the end of 2024. It will feature a port rotation of Yantian-Ningbo-Busan-Seattle-Vancouver, and the first sailing will be the departure of the 6,000 teu GSL Dorothea from Yantian on 13 December.
It has not revealed which other vessels will be deployed on the string, but previous iterations of the Mustang service have deployed between five and seven vessels.

Einride expects to end 2027 bringing in revenue at an annualized pace of about $250 million, with more than 65% of it covered by signed customer contracts. The Swedish autonomous and electric freight company gave the outlook Wednesday in its third-quarter business update . Contracted annual recurring revenue reached about $167 million as of November, up 76% from $95 million at the end of June.
Longer-term growth rests on highway autonomy, and Einride is building that system on a driving model it doesn’t have to train from scratch. The company said in October it would adapt Nvidia’s Alpamayo driving model with data from its own freight network. It expects the step to shorten development cycles and lower the cost of extending its system to new vehicle types and routes.
“You have a lot of companies that started with this route before us, who built their own proprietary AI model, and they spent billions, literally billions of dollars to train them to a state where they are now,” Henrik Green, Einride’s chief technology officer, told FreightWaves in a Nov. 13 interview. Green said such models are starting to become available to other companies, giving Einride a “highly capable, almost ready” starting point that he likened to a gold mine.
Third-quarter revenue rose 27% from the second quarter to SEK 185.9 million ($18.3 million) on a constant-currency basis. Einride has added eight customers since June, bringing its total to more than 40. It reaffirmed second-half revenue guidance of $39 million to $42 million. The company expects to exit December at an annualized run rate of $85 million to $95 million, up from about $76 million at the end of September and $49 million in December 2025.
The fleet includes more than 260 electric trucks and 10 autonomous trucks, according to the release. “About four percent of our mix is fully autonomous,” Green said, adding that five of the autonomous trucks are in Europe and five are in the U.S.
In September, Einride and Lidl put what the companies called the first cab-less SAE Level 4 truck into daily operation on a German public road. It runs under a permit from Germany’s Federal Motor Transport Authority. Einride also runs two cab-less trucks for EASE Logistics in daily freight service in Marysville, Ohio . Cumulative driverless hours in contracted customer operations reached about 8,500 as of Nov. 13, up from about 5,400 in June.
Einride moves its driver to Nvidia Hyperion
Under a collaboration announced in September , Einride is building the next generation of the Einride Driver on Nvidia’s Hyperion platform. Green said the platform gives Einride access to lidar, cameras, and radar sensors that automotive suppliers already make in high volume for Hyperion. “We’re accessing standard components that gives us quality and cost competitiveness on those sensors,” he said.
The onboard computer pairs two Nvidia Duel Thor chips. Nvidia does not sell onboard computers, so Einride buys them from Tier 1 suppliers, he said. He said those parts are also ready for vehicle type approval once the company scales up.
Training Alpamayo on freight data
Green said Einride is starting from the 34-billion-parameter version of Alpamayo, which he described as “basically a robotaxi model.” Einride will distill it to about 1 billion parameters to run inside the truck. The two-chip setup gives Einride “enough power to run a one-billion-parameter AI inside the vehicle,” he said. The company plans a live road test in the second half of 2027.
PlusAI, which develops Level 4 autonomous trucking software, said in March it is also adapting Alpamayo for heavy-duty trucks on Hyperion.
To adapt the model for trucks, Einride will fit sensors to its human-driven electric trucks and use them as data-collection vehicles. Green said a truck fitted with sensors can gather about 5 terabytes of data per hour, though much of it is curated, annotated, or dropped. Those trucks keep “producing freight capacity for our customers, for our shippers, and earning revenue to us” while they collect it, he said.
“We get that data for free, if you will, and we can train the remaining part of the model, and boom, we have a complete system,” Green said.
The current system, which Green called “Einride 1.0,” stays in place as a safety layer around the AI. That system earned Einride its public road permits, he said. The release puts those at four countries and five U.S. states for operation without a safety driver. “With that sort of safety wrapper around the AI, we can continue to deploy using that as the public road permit enabler,” Green said.
Once Alpamayo is trained for trucks, Einride could deploy it on up to 80% of its current network, Green said. The company targets highway autonomy from the first half of 2028.
Cash falls and loss outlook widens
Cash fell to SEK 533 million ($53 million) on Sept. 30 from SEK 748 million ($77 million) on June 30. Adjusted EBITDA, a non-IFRS measure, was a loss of $20.3 million in the quarter on a constant-currency basis. The company now expects a second-half adjusted EBITDA loss of $39 million to $41 million, compared with its previous outlook of $35 million to $37 million.
On a reported basis, third-quarter net profit was $95.3 million, driven by a $133.8 million gain on financial instruments measured at fair value. The company excludes that gain from adjusted EBITDA. The quarterly figures are preliminary and unaudited. The release also says contracted annual recurring revenue is subject to termination rights and management assumptions and is not a revenue forecast.
Most of the 500 Tesla Semis Einride ordered in August are due to go into service in 2027, with asset-backed financing paying for fleet growth.
“We are taking a disciplined approach to growth, using third-party financing to expand our fleet while investing our own capital in technology and operations,” Anubhav Verma, Einride’s chief financial officer, said in the release.
The company still targets cash-flow breakeven in 2028 with 1,500 to 2,000 vehicles in operation. By 2030, it aims for more than $2 billion in annualized run-rate revenue. That goal includes converting about $800 million in potential long-term annual recurring revenue from non-binding joint business plans with customers. Einride plans to move to full quarterly reporting with detailed financial statements in 2027.
Today the Einride Driver runs on the company’s own cab-less trucks. Einride is also integrating it into DAF’s electric truck platform, with software integration and commissioning scheduled for 2027.
“What you will see going forward is the ability to generalize across form factors, across different kinds of traffic situation, different countries, different geographies,” Green said.
Why it matters: Autonomous truck developers that built their own driving models now compete with a company adapting Nvidia’s model on data from trucks already earning freight revenue. Einride’s Alpamayo road test in the second half of 2027 will show whether that route cuts the cost of reaching highway autonomy.

Warehouse automation is trending — and rightfully so. Robotics and software systems solve many operational bottlenecks amid growing order volumes. They also mitigate the impact of chronic labor shortages .
What’s Related
Decision-makers should continue adopting digital technology . However, the shift to automation shouldn’t come at the expense of physical infrastructure . Here’s how prudent executives modernize tangible warehouse design elements for workplace safety and security .
1. Color-coded floor markings to guide traffic
The United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration requires appropriate markings on permanent aisles and passageways used by material handling equipment, such as forklifts. However, the agency doesn’t specify how wide the lines should be or what colors to use.
Following industry standards is a safe bet. For example, ANSI Z535.1 recommends orange for warning labels and yellow to communicate caution. This standard is a handy guide when color-coding aisles, traffic lanes, general walkways, equipment locations, inspection areas and other key zones across the warehouse floor.
RELATED: How to Set Up Warehouse Automation Without the Big Price Tag
2. Mirrors to improve visibility around blind spots
Mounting parabolic or convex mirrors makes traffic paths, loading bays and personnel exit points safer. The curvature of these mirrors expands fields of view, which can help reduce blind spots and raise situational awareness among workers.
These safety mirrors come in different configurations. Generally, quarter or 90-degree domes suit sharp bends. Half or 180-degree mirrors fit T-intersections, while full or 360-degree domes increase visibility in cross aisles when suspended from the ceiling.
3. Upgraded dock doors to handle heavy daily use
Commercial doors in warehouses and distribution centers have a demanding job. Busy loading environments require high-cycle door systems to withstand the rigors of heavy daily use. Industrial facilities often benefit from insulated sectional steel panels, which maintain consistent indoor temperature levels and protect inventory from dust and the elements.
Integrating a commercial door operator is key to streamlining loading and unloading operations. Models with sensors can detect obstructions and automatically reverse to prevent accidental closures.
4. Column barriers to protect racking systems
These barriers absorb impact, helping keep racking posts intact when hit by forklifts, pallet jacks and transport vehicles. More warehouses have high clear heights to accommodate taller racks and support modern distribution.
Column barriers avert disaster, especially in facilities with autonomous mobile robots that can navigate independently across the floor and crash into racks. Too much inventory may fall if a multilevel storage structure collapses after an accidental collision. Wraparound protectors can trap debris and moisture, though, so routine inspections and periodic cleaning are essential.
5. Bollards to safeguard entrances and traffic areas
These sturdy vertical posts protect commercial properties from ram-raiding. A good case in point was a ram raid at an Australian shopping center, where bollards stopped a truck used by thieves that targeted an ATM inside the mall.
When properly placed, spaced and finished, bollards should be easily visible to forklift operators and freight vehicle drivers. At the same time, pedestrians should be able to pass through them with ease. Security landscaping features can complement bollards. Thoughtfully placed natural boulders, reinforced planters and concealed ditches can help keep unauthorized vehicles at bay.
Modern warehouses need strong physical infrastructure, too
Investing heavily in automated systems and industrial robots increases the need for better physical infrastructure. Color-coded floor markings, parabolic mirrors, insulated, high-cycle loading doors, column barriers and bollards should be high on the agenda of warehouse operations managers who value increased workplace safety and security.
Dan Parks is a senior writer at Modded.com with six years of experience specializing in supply chain content.

Military-Spec Defender Begins Showing Off in Front of the British Army
15 photos
Photo: Land Rover
It's been only a few months since British carmaker Land Rover rolled out something called the Wolf Series II, or Wolf II. Basically the military version of the current generation Defender, it has now begun trials in front of the British military, as it competes for the Ministry of Defense's attention in the Light Mobility Vehicle program, pitted against no less than six other competitors.
Land Rover announced this week that it has enlisted three variants of the fresh Wolf II for the trials that are taking place at the Millbrook proving ground in Bedfordshire: the General‑Purpose Vehicle, Battlefield Ambulance, and Tactical Mobility Vehicle.
They all share the same underpinnings, meaning the same D7x aluminum monocoque architecture that is also used on the civilian Defender, but also the D7X‑R that snatched the win in the Stock category at the 2026 Dakar Rally. This choice was made because, as per the manufacturer, its torsional rigidity is three times higher than on body‑on‑frame designs.
The company doesn't specifically say this, but we're probably dealing with the same powertrain as well, all of that hidden in a purpose‑engineered body that looks a lot like what we know from the roads.
Without going into too many details, Defender says that, before coming out with the design, it performed 62,000 tests and covered millions of miles in the harshest conditions our planet has to offer, going from minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit) in the Arctic to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) in the desert. Why, the vehicle was even taken as high as 10,000 feet (3,000 meters) in the Rocky Mountains in Colorado.
That makes everything the Millbrook proving ground has to throw at it pale by comparison, but that doesn't mean the military doesn't need to see it in action. The Defender, along with its competitors, will now spend three months there, being assessed for military use.
Named Wolf in honor of the British military vehicles that have been called so since 1998, the family of battle-ready SUVs includes, aside from the three versions mentioned above, a utility derivative as well. It's unclear why this one is not part of the trials.
Regardless of what happens at Millbrook, Land Rover plans to release more military variants in the near future. It also plans to pitch the designs to allied nations - after all, there are over 600,000 Defenders of various kinds in service of some 100 nations.
For the British soldiers to start using them for their purposes, though, the Wolf II will have to outsmart and outperform vehicles made by Ineos, Rheinmetall, Babcock, General Dynamics Land Systems, NP Aerospace, and Iturri. We'll keep an eye on things and let you know how it goes.

Truck cameras long served fleets after a crash, as evidence to reconstruct what happened and size up their exposure in court. Carriers including Werner Enterprises now use that AI-powered video and telematics data to spot risky driving and coach it out before a crash.
Executives from Werner and Bennett Family of Companies described the shift last month on a Motive-hosted panel at the American Trucking Associations’ Management Conference & Exhibition in Charlotte, North Carolina. Austin Henderson is vice president of innovation and engineering at Werner, which bought dedicated carrier FirstFleet for $245 million in January . Jared Whitson is senior director of safety and compliance at Bennett. Both fleets use Motive’s AI platform technology.
“When I started this process, it was, OK, well, how do we do accident reconstruction? How do we know what our exposure is in the case of litigation?” Henderson said of his fleet’s camera program. “That quickly has evolved into how do we prevent the litigation?”
Prevention means reading the signals drivers send through telemetry and on-road events, he said, so the fleet can retrain a driver or, in some cases, separate from one.
“If we’re not leveraging the AI, you can rest assured that plaintiff’s attorneys know how to leverage the AI,” Henderson said.
The concern is showing up in carrier survey data. Motor carriers ranked lawsuit abuse reform as their top concern in the American Transportation Research Institute’s 2026 Critical Issues in the Trucking Industry report , released Oct. 18. Across all respondents, lawsuit abuse held the No. 2 spot for a second straight year, behind fuel prices .
In-cab alerts reach drivers in real time
Gary Johnson, Motive’s head of safety and compliance strategy, moderated the panel. In the older model, he said, a camera captured video and the back office reviewed it later. Motive’s approach for what it calls physical AI is AI-powered detection and intervention in real time, with people still overseeing the system.
Henderson’s fleet runs only outward-facing cameras. He said Motive built a distracted-driving alert that works from those cameras alone, at the fleet’s request. When it fires, the driver gets an alert in the cab, the back office gets one too, and staff call the driver to direct him to a safe place.
One driver his team brought to a safety stop called back the next day after watching the video. “You may have saved my life, because I was not aware of what was happening,” the driver said, according to Henderson.
Video clears a driver who initially opposed it
The same footage protects drivers who are not at fault. Henderson described a driver with about 20 years and 2 million miles who was “quite antagonistic about the cameras being installed.”
Two weeks after the camera went in, the driver was involved in a highway incident that the replay showed was not his fault.
“Two days later, he gets served. Two days later after that, we get notice,” Henderson said. “That takes about four days to resolve because the driver was clearly in the right.”
That driver now appears in the fleet’s training videos, telling other drivers he initially opposed the cameras and showing them what happened.
Coaching moves to the same day
At Henderson’s fleet, drivers cannot move forward in their workflow until they watch the video of a flagged event. He said around like 97% of those videos are reviewed the day they occur.
“So that means the driver’s not waiting a week, two weeks to go with a coach to work through a stop sign they ran two weeks ago,” Henderson said. “If that’s your process, that’s way too long.”
The coaching is partly automated. The fleet has loaded AI avatars of its regional safety managers into Motive’s coaching tool and tells drivers the videos are AI-produced. Henderson said he got one himself the morning of the panel, on a close-following event from the week before.
“Good drivers really want to be great drivers,” he said. “They don’t want to be caught tailgating.”
Compliance review drops to seconds
At Bennett, Whitson described the change in the compliance office. Researching a single hours-of-service event used to take four or five minutes to decide whether it was a violation. AI now delivers a recommendation with its reasoning, and staff confirm it or reject it.
“So it’s taking that [review] down from four or five minutes per event to literally 30 seconds maybe,” Whitson said.
He said he does not expect much realignment on the compliance floor at first. Staff will “get to the things that they haven’t been able to get to for a long time that just fell off the edge,” he said.
Bennett has also tied fault codes to its shops. When a truck with a critical fault code crosses a geofence at one of them, the system sends a notification. Whitson said a future version could set up the repair or work order itself. For now, Bennett’s first Motive AI Agents only notify staff .
Legacy systems slow the rollout
But challenges remain. Asked for an example of AI acting on the road, Whitson said Bennett is “not that far down that road.”
Whitson cautioned against “the blind acceptance and just going all in.”
“It has to earn our trust, and it has to keep our trust,” he said.
Henderson said older systems on both the Werner and FirstFleet sides limit how quickly new tools can be wired together.
“Plumbing’s really boring until it doesn’t work,” he said.
Both executives said smaller carriers could have an edge because they have less legacy technology to drag forward. Two years ago, Whitson said, a small fleet would have lacked the resources for projects like these.
“I would say you could have a 25-truck fleet. You could have a two-person office,” Whitson said. “And you could run that office like it’s staffed by 20 people at this point.”
Henderson’s advice for a small carrier is to “pick a provider and lean in as hard as you can.”
“I promise you, in five years, it’s going to look drastically different than it does right now,” he said. “We’re probably going to have conversations that we didn’t even imagine were possible.”
Why it matters: Truck AI dash cams used to help fleets reconstruct crashes and size their lawsuit exposure. Werner and Bennett are now using the same data from Motive for same-day coaching and real-time alerts. It’s now a difference between defending a claim and preventing the crash that triggers it.

Artificial intelligence is playing a bigger role in business decisions, but most leaders still want a person to make the final call. In a new Körber repo rt , 73% of executives surveyed said they were uncomfortable letting technology have the final say.
What’s Related
Among U.S. respondents, 77% said AI was more involved in decisions, and 78% said decision-making had become more complex. Across the full survey, nearly three-quarters said too much data could make decisions harder or that decisions could stall while teams waited for information.
Körber released its AI and Decision Complexity Report on Nov. 18. Censuswide surveyed 2,000 senior leaders, split evenly between the U.S. and Germany, at organizations with more than $250 million in annual revenue and at least 250 employees.
Supply chain leads on AI use
Supply chain and distribution leaders reported the highest AI involvement in decisions, at 92%. Handling exceptions and dealing with variability were challenges for 36% of respondents, while 24% cited trouble getting systems to work together.
Healthcare and life sciences leaders reported slower AI adoption, at 60%. Their most frequently cited challenges were connecting systems (48%) and workforce skills (46%). Körber based each industry breakdown on responses from 50 U.S. executives.
RELATED: 10 Routine Supply Chain Tasks You Should Use AI For
AI spending plans are similar
About 59% of leaders at organizations making companywide changes planned to invest heavily in AI tools that help people make decisions. The share was nearly identical among organizations still in the pilot phase.
Leaders in the companywide group were more likely to say their organizations were performing well, at 64% compared with 42% in the pilot group.
“Most organizations are planning or executing significant AI-related investments, but spending alone won’t secure a return on investment ,” said Helena Garriga, a member of Körber’s executive board and president of its supply chain business.
Four things that help AI pay off
Körber points to four things companies can put in place to get more out of their AI spending.
Timely, reliable data that reaches teams when they need to act.
Clear responsibility for who makes the final call and when.
A process for handling exceptions that need human judgment.
Human oversight based on the decision, with clear rules for what can run automatically and what needs approval.

Credit: Korean Air
By Alex Lennane
20 November 2026
Korean Air expects its available belly cargo capacity to rise 20% when it integrates Asiana Airlines on 17 December, giving it more room to bring freight from across Asia into Incheon to connect with long-haul services.
The expansion comes after a third quarter in which Korean Air’s standalone cargo revenue rose 34.3% year on year, to ₩1.43tn ($1.05bn) , according to its preliminary results.
Cargo traffic, measured in cargo tonne-km, increased 5.3% against a 4% increase in capacity, while yields climbed 27.5%. Compared with the second quarter, however, cargo yields fell 10.5%, while traffic rose 3.8%.
For the first nine months, cargo revenue was up 28%, to ₩4.06tn. The airline cited steady demand for AI and semiconductor shipments, alongside time-sensitive cargo ranging from solar equipment to fresh eggs.
Jaedong Eum, EVP and head of Korean Air’s cargo business division, told The Loadstar the airline would unify cargo sales, bookings, and handling worldwide on the day the combined carrier launched.
“On 17 December, all domestic and international cargo handling contracts, booking platforms, and sales systems will be completely unified,” he said. “Freight will be sold, booked, and handled entirely under the integrated Korean Air banner worldwide.”
Asiana’s short- and medium-haul Asian routes will feed Korean Air’s long-haul network through Incheon, with the combined passenger network serving more than 110 destinations. Mr Eum said transhipments from elsewhere in Asia already accounted for a “significant majority” of Korean Air’s total cargo volume, although he gave no split for AI-related shipments or a breakdown of the extra belly capacity by route.
One addition to the Asian network is Clark, in the Philippines, among 11 international routes served by Asiana alone that will move into the Korean Air network, according to ChosunBiz . It also reported that the combined carrier planned to increase Incheon-New York passenger flights from three to four a day.
Asiana’s freighter business was sold to Air Incheon, now AirZeta, in August 2025 as a condition of merger approval. Korean Air’s own fleet of 23 freighters includes 12 777Fs, seven 747-8Fs and four other 747 freighters. Mr Eum said the airline prioritised its main decks for heavy, outsized, and specialist shipments, such as AI infrastructure, and used passenger bellies for high-frequency ecommerce and express parcels.
Where the technology freight comes from
“The global expansion of data centres is serving as a primary growth engine for our cargo business,” said Mr Eum. “We are seeing sustained, high-volume demand for IT infrastructure components, particularly server racks, semiconductors, and advanced batteries.
“The supply chain is highly regionalised: we are moving server hardware originating from China and South-east Asia, semiconductor equipment and advanced batteries from Japan, and high-end semiconductor chips and power supply infrastructure originating right here in Korea.”
That traffic is concentrated on transpacific routes serving North American tech hubs. The Americas accounted for 38% of Korean Air’s Q3 cargo route revenue, up from 35% a year earlier. Mr Eum did not quantify the airline’s growth in AI-related tonnage, but pointed to IATA data showing Asia-North America cargo traffic rose 17% year on year in September, its eighth consecutive month of growth, against 7.7% globally.
“Entering the traditional November peak season, we are experiencing compounded capacity pressure on the Transpacific, driven by overlapping traditional Q4 consumer goods shipments and robust, year-round AI-related hardware demand,” he said. “Consequently, we are maximising our Asia-to-Americas capacity.”
Europe-bound space was under less pressure, as cross-border ecommerce growth moderated, he added. The airline is seeking more Europe-to-Asia freight to balance loads. On US routes, where Mr Eum described a more pronounced imbalance, Korean Air is adjusting services and focusing on yields.
Korean Air said it planned to use extra flights and charters on routes where it expected strong year-end demand. It also identified French wine and South American cherries as seasonal traffic it was targeting, alongside livestock charters and shipments for overseas factory expansions.
Pharma helps offset softer ecommerce
Changes to trade and customs rules had slowed the growth of parcels originating in China, Mr Eum said. Volumes had since stabilised as shippers adapted their customs clearance procedures.
“Any softening in general ecommerce has been comprehensively offset by our strategic pivot toward specialised cargo verticals,” he said.
“Concurrently, we are seeing strong, sustained growth in pharmaceuticals and cold-chain logistics, fuelled by global biopharma R&D and expanding domestic investments in biosimilar manufacturing facilities.” He also pointed to steady growth in exports of Korean beauty products and goods tied to Korean popular culture.
Incheon and JFK upgrades
At Incheon, Korean Air has replaced its elevating transfer vehicles, introduced automated guided vehicles, and added a second outbound bypass line. Dispatch capacity on the bypass rose from 18 to 30 unit load devices an hour, while overall terminal handling capacity increased 25%, according to Mr Eum.
He said truck bottlenecks had eased and cargo handovers were faster, although he gave no before-and-after timings.
“Post-renovation, the vast majority of our historical bottleneck issues have been resolved, with pressure now limited only to the most extreme peak acceptance windows,” he said.
Korean Air is targeting 2027 for completion of a major renovation of its JFK cargo terminal. It has also announced a daily Incheon-Newark passenger service from 22 May, using a 777-300ER.
Fifteen new freighters on order
Korean Air finalised an order including eight 777-8 freighters in September, and converted seven A350-1000 passenger aircraft orders to A350Fs last year. Mr Eum framed the investment as a way to reduce fuel burn, emissions, and operating costs.
“Our maindeck investment strategy is fundamentally driven by fleet modernisation, unit-cost efficiency, and sustainability, rather than sheer capacity,” he explained.
Korean Air’s standalone fuel bill rose 67% year on year in Q3. Mr Eum identified persistently high fuel prices and geopolitical volatility as the biggest risks for 2027, saying the airline was optimising long-haul flight paths and minimising technical stops to contain costs.
He sees high-value technology and pharma as the strongest opportunities for next year. “We do not view this as a cyclical peak,” he said of AI-related demand.
“The integration of AI chips and the subsequent build-out of global data centres represents a structural, long-term capital expenditure cycle by big tech firms, ensuring sustainable freight demand.”

Time Capsule Mustang Boss 302 Is a 1-in-3 Unicorn, Rare Factory Options Hiding in Plain Sight
63 photos
Photo: Facebook/Nate's Classic Cars
Unrestored muscle cars retaining factory paint rarely survive intact, making a 1970 Ford Mustang Boss 302 all the more special. Extra special. Especially special. Add the Calypso Coral SportsRoof paired with a white vinyl interior, and those 71,624 miles of authentic history are ignorable. As if the fact that it’s a time capsule Boss 302, it’s also a solid driver. What more could you ask for? “The keys” is a good answer.
Verified through paint-meter readings, the factory Calypso Coral lacquer remains untouched save for minor spot blending on the passenger-side rear quarter end cap. Honest patina appears in slight edge thinning along the fenders, fine chips and hairline cracks across the matte-black Boss 302 hockey-stick side stripes, and subtle weathering on the original chrome bumpers.
Original Carlite glass, Trico stainless wiper blades, the 1970 single-headlamp grille, and a blacked-out taillight panel complete the menu. For 56 years and counting, this Son of Trans Am doesn’t look like it’s seen ten Presidents come and go.
Equally compelling is the generous roster of Marti Report–documented options adorning this fastback. A functional matte-black Shaker hood scoop rises through the center stripe, complemented by rear-window Sport Slats on chrome hinges above the blacked-out decklid panel.
Photo: YouTube/Nate's Classic Cars Matching matte-black rear and chin spoilers, color-keyed racing mirrors, and optional 15-by-7-inch chrome Magnum 500 wheels wrapped in Goodyear Polyglas GT F60-15 raised-white-letter tires give the survivor total street presence.
Beneath the hood sits a numbers-matching 302-cubic-inch V8 mated to its original 4-speed manual gearbox and rear axle. Authentic touches include the blue Shaker air cleaner and snorkel, cast-aluminum finned valve covers, fender-mounted factory rev limiter, intact buck tag, original cooling fan, and period-correct Motorcraft service ignition parts.
Inside the trunk rest the original speckled mat, F78-14 Space Saver spare, jack, factory decals, quarter-panel sound deadener, Panduit wiring clips, and decklid prop rod.
Inside, original white vinyl high-back bucket seats show subtle age yellowing alongside matching door panels, manual cranks, black carpet, original belts, dash VIN tag, and door sticker. Options include a center console, an 8,000-rpm tachometer, and a factory AM radio beside an engraved aluminum Hurst T-handle shifter. The small-block fires instantly with a throaty dual-exhaust bark, pulling cleanly through fourth gear and stopping straight with surefooted braking.
Photo: YouTube/Nate's Classic Cars In 1970, only 33 fastback Mustangs had a Calypso Coral livery and a white interior, and eight of those were Boss 302s. If the Magnum 500 wheels on this car are original equipment, than the rarity drops to one in three Boss 302s ordered with the color combo, rear deck spoiler, and Mag 500s.
It was the best money could buy in 1970, and it’s still a thrill today, except one needs a lot more cash now than back when these were just ”Mustangs”. Ford developed the model in 1969 for factory homologation to go racing in the Trans American Championship.
The designer who penned the C3 Corvette, Larry Shinoda, was tasked with the Boss Mustang program, and it was he who gently avoided curious inquiries about the secretive car by calling it "the Boss' car." He was referring to Semon Knudsen, Ford’s top brass hat, who was committed to put FoMoCo ahead of Chevrolet in racing, not just in showrooms.
Photo: YouTube/Nate's Classic Cars The name stuck, uniting three classic icons—the 1969–1970 Boss 302, the NASCAR-focused 1969–1970 Boss 429, and the 1971 Boss 351—before returning for a celebrated two-year revival in 2012 and 2013.
Whereas the Boss 429 existed to qualify a big-block for NASCAR, the Boss 302 was engineered as a balanced road-racing homologation special for the Sports Car Club of America's Over 2-Liter Trans-Am series. Particularly, it was the factory answer to Chevy’s own Camaro Z/28, the car that had snatched the title in ’68, and it would do it again in 1969.
The Boss 302’s upgrades added reinforced shock towers, stiffer springs, staggered rear shocks, front disc brakes, 16:1 steering, a chin spoiler, and—for 1970—revised front and rear sway bars plus redesigned dual exhausts.
Photo: YouTube/Nate's Classic Cars Production remained low (especially compared to the enormously popular Z/28) across every Boss era. Ford built the original Boss 302 for two model years: 1,628 units in 1969 and 7,013 in 1970, totaling 8,641 cars. Its big brother was rarer still, with 859 Boss 429s in 1969 and 499 in 1970—1,358 total—plus 1,806 Boss 351s in 1971. Decades later, Ford delivered 4,017 revived Boss 302s in 2012 and 4,318 in 2013, including Laguna Seca models, totaling 8,335.
Powering the 1969–1970 Boss 302 was a hybrid 302-cubic-inch (4.9-liter) V8 mating a strengthened Windsor block with free-breathing Cleveland cylinder heads, heavy-duty connecting rods, and a four-barrel carburetor. Rated at 290 horsepower at 5,800 rpm and 290 pound-feet at 4,300 rpm, it paired strictly with a Toploader 4-speed manual and 3.50, 3.91, or 4.30 rear gears.
Showroom pricing reflected that competition hardware without alienating street buyers. In 1969, the Boss 302 debuted at $3,588, an $865 premium over a standard Mustang Fastback with the regular 220-horsepower 302 two-barrel V8 at $2,723. For 1970, Ford set the Boss 302 base price at $3,720—$848 above a regular 302-equipped Fastback at $2,872—while options like the Shaker hood, Sport Slats, rear spoiler, tachometer, and Magnum 500 wheels lifted well-equipped cars past $4,000.
Photo: YouTube/Nate's Classic Cars Road tests promptly justified that sticker. Ford's 290-horsepower rating proved modest—engineer Bill Barr measured 314 horsepower fully dressed and 390 stripped on the dyno. Contemporary tests clocked 0 to 60 mph in 6.9 seconds and quarter-mile passes of 14.4 to 14.6 seconds at 98 to 100.5 mph. together with a 118-mph top speed, the Boss 302 prompted Car and Driver to hail it as the best-handling Mustang up to that point.
Motorsport cemented that reputation. Fielded in Trans-Am by Bud Moore Engineering—with Shelby American also competing in 1969—the Boss 302 debuted with Parnelli Jones winning Michigan's stormy 1969 opener before trailing Penske's Camaros.
Returning for 1970 in school-bus yellow, Bud Moore's cars driven by Jones and George Follmer captured six of 11 races, including Laguna Seca, Mid-Ohio, and Jones's battered-fender Riverside finale, securing Ford's 1970 SCCA Trans-Am Manufacturers' Championship and Jones's drivers' title.
Photo: YouTube/Nate's Classic Cars The car we see in Nate Jones's video is rare for more reasons than one: the emblem is the obvious one, the survivor condition is the second, and the color combo is a close third. Together, these traits add up to the asking price of $105,000. It’s quite the markup over the past 12 months median for similar cars. Hagerty pegs comparable Excellent-condition cars at $99,600.
For perspective, the priciest street-legal Boss 302 sold publicly reached $258,500 at Mecum Kissimmee in 2022, whereas a 1970 Trans-Am racer brought $407,000 at Gooding in 2009. Maybe this survivor isn’t all that expensive, after all. At the same Mecum 2022 auction, one very similar to it (same color combo, with rear deck spoiler and Magnum 500s, went for $200k hammer price ($220,000 including buyer’s fines).

© Daliscot55
By Nils Roche
20 November 2026
A study for European shipowners puts shipping’s annual EU ETS bill at about €9bn, at €100 a tonne. The same study finds that d irective does not oblige member states to send any fixed share of that money back to shipping, and names only France and Estonia as exceptions. Delegates carry that experience into London on Monday, when ISWG-GHG 23 opens and they try again to fix a global carbon price for the same industry. The weak point of the draft a year ago was the money. It still is.
Last year’s blanks, this year’s deadline
The Net-Zero Framework was approved in April 2025. In October, adoption was adjourned by a year, by 57 votes to 49, with 21 abstentions, after US cabinet members threatened visa penalties, port fees, and sanctions against net-zero supporters. ISWG-GHG 22 in September closed without a compromise text. The next window is short: the working group meets from 23 to 27 November, MEPC 85 follows from 30 November, and the extraordinary session is due to resume on 4 December, if MEPC confirms it.
The draft still does not say whether the money sits in an IMO fund or with governments, or under what rules it is distributed. The method for rewarding zero and near-zero fuels is due by 1 March 2027. The $100 and $380 remedial unit prices are fixed only to 2030, and the post-2030 mechanism is due by 1 January 2028. Delegates would vote on a price signal and write the rules for its proceeds afterwards.
Meanwhile, US opposition remains vocal. Laura DiBella, Federal Maritime Commission chair, told the IBIA convention in New York last week that the NZF “cannot be adopted, will never be enforced”.
She added that the US will not accept the IMO fund, and that any financial mechanism should sit under member states’ authority. She further cited FMC analysis putting the fund’s cost to shipping at $53bn to $265bn a year which, frankly, is hard to support – published estimates of its revenue are $10bn to $15bn, and I could not trace the FMC figure to a published method. The FMC’s Section 19 powers include fees of up to $1m a voyage. It has not used them.
Most governments are poorly placed to vote for a new charge on trade now. Brent traded above $100 in September and was near $92 this week, following Gulf disruptions that lifted bunker costs for most of the year. The negotiators are mostly maritime administration officials and secretariat staff who do not face voters. Ministers entered the debate in October 2025, when three US secretaries signed a retaliation statement. That is my reading of the politics, not a poll.
What carriers have already learned
Carriers’ general position rests on two European precedents. The ETS shows what happens to a levy’s proceeds when nothing binds them. The directive requires climate spending in general, not spending on shipping. A carve-out of about 2.5 million allowances applies to maritime in 2026, and it declines each year. The commission’s 2025 Carbon Market Report found member states put around 5% of 2024 revenues into industrial decarbonisation, despite a legal requirement to do so. That figure covers all sectors, but it shows how little a spending rule constrains a treasury.
FuelEU is built the opposite way. Deficit ships pay surplus holders, so the money stays inside shipping and rewards the owners that burned cleaner fuel. It worked for owners that invested, until fuel prices shifted the arithmetic. With VLSFO dearer, B100 in Rotterdam traded $133 a tonne below it on 2 November, which makes surplus cheap to generate. The OceanScore pooling index stood at €180 to €230 a tonne in autumn 2025 and at €80.45 on 2 November. Demand for surplus is fixed by the regulation, so extra supply sets a lower price. ENGINE also cites new sellers and surplus outpacing demand after the summer, so fuel prices are not the only cause.
The NZF takes FuelEU’s promise of a reward and the ETS’s route for the money. Remedial unit payments go to an IMO fund, and the zero and near-zero reward is paid from that fund by a method not yet written. A reward set after the vote, on a price that can fall as FuelEU’s did, is a risk carriers would be accepting in advance. The sovereign alternative that Washington prefers is the ETS model again.
The strongest objection
IMO regimes are usually finished after adoption, and waiting for perfect text means no framework.
Without one, Brussels keeps its own rules. FuelEU’s review clause requires an evaluation by the end of 2027, and the ETS directive requires a EC report on wider coverage, if there is no global measure by 2028. A level playing field is a fair demand, and it is the carriers’ best argument for adopting something.
It does not settle the question of whose money this is.
A framework with no rules for its proceeds is global in name only. Carriers would still face the ETS and FuelEU, since the deduction mechanics in the commission’s July proposals remain unclear, and they would have no vote on the fund. States vote at the IMO. Industry has consultative status and no vote. The useful ask is narrower than adoption or rejection: written fund rules, a reward method and a post-2030 price path, delivered before the vote.
Without them, “global or nothing” can deliver a global levy on top of the regional ones, with no say over where any of it goes.

Rockwell Automation has agreed to buy AGILOX, an Austrian maker of driverless forklifts, from private equity firm Carlyle. Rockwell says the deal would more than double its autonomous mobile robot (AMR) business.
What’s Related
The companies announced the agreement on Wednesday. Carlyle took a majority stake in AGILOX in 2021.
Rockwell expects the deal to close in the quarter ending March 31, subject to regulatory approval and other closing conditions. AGILOX would join Rockwell’s Intelligent Devices segment.
Forklifts meet flatbeds
The big draw for Rockwell is how AGILOX fits with OTTO, the AMR line it added when it bought Clearpath Robotics in 2023. AGILOX makes forklift robots that move pallets. OTTO is best known for its flatbed robots and already sells a driverless forklift. The deal would give Rockwell more models for moving pallets.
There’s a geographic fit too. OTTO is strongest in North America, while AGILOX has an established base in Europe. AGILOX also gets a door into Rockwell’s customers in consumer packaged goods and life sciences.
“Combining AGILOX and OTTO technologies creates a best-in-class technology platform,” said Blake Moret, Rockwell’s chairman and CEO.
He added that the deal “doesn’t just combine strengths; it amplifies innovation and delivers breakthrough value for our customers.”
Who is AGILOX?
Founded in 2017 and based in Neukirchen bei Lambach, Austria, AGILOX has deployed more than 2,500 AMRs for customers in automotive , third-party logistics , food and beverage , and pharmaceuticals . It has more than 250 employees and subsidiaries in Europe, the U.S. and China .
Carlyle says AGILOX has more than 400 customers worldwide and works with more than 40 partners across more than 35 countries. The firm also says AGILOX’s revenue has quadrupled since its 2021 investment.
AGILOX co-CEOs and co-founders Dirk Erlacher and David Niedermaier said the deal gives the company room to grow.
“For AGILOX, joining Rockwell Automation represents a transformational step forward,” they said. “This gives AGILOX the scale and market reach that we couldn’t build on our own.”

Ram Wants a Piece of Toyota Tacoma and Ford Maverick Sales With New Dakota and Rampage Trucks
11 photos
Photo: Ram
Ford has moved 135,147 examples of the Maverick in the United States through October 2026, all while Toyota Tacoma sales reached 237,128 units during the ten-month period. That difference should tell anyone still dismissing unibody compact pickups and body-on-frame midsizers, and Ram has noticed how truck customers are voting with their wallets.
The South American-built Rampage is the Stellantis-controlled brand's ticket into a segment where the Blue Oval is king right now, while the return of the Dakota will help Ram fight Toyota's dominance of the mid-size pickup truck segment. Courting buyers who want an open bed and tougher styling than you get in a compact crossover, the Rampage is a very promising model for the US market.
With the Rampage, the Ram brand has little in the way of competition due to Hyundai discontinuing the poor-selling Santa Cruz, effectively leaving the Maverick and Rampage alone. The redesigned Dakota will have a harder time proving its worth, for the mid-size truck segment has a few popular models.
Beyond the Tacoma, customer demand for the Nissan Frontier and Chevrolet Colorado can be considered healthy. Both the Rampage and the Dakota should arrive in 2028, according to Ram chief executive officer Matt VanDyke.
Speaking to MoparInsiders, the big kahuna also hinted at performance-focused versions of the Dakota. The Rampage, meanwhile, is viewed as an opportunity in the growing compact pickup segment, with VanDyke steering the importance of affordability and value.
The chief exec further acknowledged that Rampage could be attractive to fleet customers and small businesses, though Ram expects retail customers to account for most sales. VanDyke does not see the Rampage as an alternative to small commercial vans like the ProMaster City, which Ram previously sold in the US with little changes from the Euro-spec Fiat Doblo.
Photo: Ram Speaking of which, the ProMaster City will return stateside for model year 2027 with Euro-centric goodies from the wider Stellantis group. Think of the redesigned van as the twin of the Fiat Scudo, a.k.a. Opel and Vauxhall Vivaro, Peugeot Expert, and Citroen Jumpy.
The biggest difference over the previous-gen ProMaster City is that Ram stepped one segment up, filling the mid-size commercial van gap in the North American market. Having cleared that up, pricing will probably decide how much of a commercial success the Rampage will be in the compact segment.
Ford has already made the Maverick way pricier than it used to be, with its MSRP increasing from $19,995 for model year 2022 all the way to $28,145 for model year 2027. Part of the reason why the Maverick captured its segment is competitive pricing.
The 2027 Santa Cruz, by comparison, is listed by Hyundai Motor America at $30,300 before destination charge and other taxes. Two grand more gets you the rear-wheel-drive Frontier King Cab S, and this difference is way too small for the Hyundai to be perceived as a good deal by many peeps.
Also sold in Europe, the Rampage is produced in Brazil on Small Wide 4x4 LWB underpinnings. The platform underpinning this fellow also underpins the previous-gen Jeep Compass, Alfa Romeo Tonale, and Dodge Hornet, which is why adapting it for North America should be relatively easy.
The Dakota is expected to ride on a modified Jeep Gladiator platform, as indicated by head of design Ralph Gilles earlier this year . This, in turn, means that the 3.6-liter Pentastar V6 fits under the hood of the Dakota. Whether the folks at Ram can also make a case for V8 muscle, let's wait and see.

PARIS — The Netherlands presented a defense-industrial plan with a target to grow its defense technological and industrial base by 40% by 2030, with local defense industry revenue reaching around €15 billion ($16.5 billion).
The government has earmarked €1.6 billion for the industry plan , with a focus on integrated air and missile defense, data-driven command and digital resilience, unmanned and autonomous systems; and military sustainment.
The Netherlands is the seventh-biggest defense spender among European NATO countries, ahead of Sweden, based on data from the alliance, yet the country lacks major defense prime comparable to Sweden’s Saab, Germany’s Rheinmetall or the United Kingdom’s BAE Systems.
Still, the nation of 18 million punches above its weight in several defense technology areas. For example, France’s Thales has a large part of its radar business in the Netherlands, while the country is also home to Destinus, a defense technology company which said this week its Ruta cruise missiles were used by Ukraine to target the Kerch Strait bridge.
“Through this national program, the government, together with industry and research institutions, is rolling up its sleeves to ensure that the armed forces get what they need, both now and in a conflict situation,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament .
Warfighting is fundamentally changing, and the impact of technology is “enormous,” the government said, citing space technology, the electromagnetic spectrum, artificial intelligence, cyber, drones and long-range weapons. At the same time, the war in Ukraine has shown the importance of mass, production capability, stocks and the ability to sustain the fight, according to the government.
Strengthening the Dutch defense industry will strengthen the warfighting ability of the Dutch armed forces, according to the government. Spending on the plan will include €600 million for industrial ecosystems and scaling production, €320 million to help pay for international cooperation, and €150 million on make supply chains more resilient.
The Netherlands is counting on the domestic share of Dutch defense-industry revenue to grow faster than the industry’s overall revenue, climbing 50% by 2030 to more than €10 billion. Meanwhile, the target is for exports to grow by about 25%.
The MoD will give greater weight to the origin of products and suppliers in procurement decisions in 2027, and introduce procurement guidelines from the first quarter of 2028 that take into account the origin of raw materials and components, as well a supply-chain transparency, the government said.
The Netherlands is betting on international cooperation in the focus areas, and will actively contribute to leading groups for joint capability development with like-minded partners including Belgium, Germany, France, the U.K. and the Nordic countries, the government said.
“Thanks to their innovative capacity, the Dutch defense industry and research institutions are in a good position to play key roles in global value chains and in this way help reduce risky strategic dependencies for the Netherlands and Europe,” the government wrote in its letter to parliament.
To improve financing access for defense firms, the Ministry of Defence together with Invest-NL will set up a €200 million investment fund for dual-use companies in defense and security.
The MoD will also set up the National Institute for Defence Technology, or NIDT, in 2028, with a budget that will climb to €350 million a year by 2030, the government said. The goal of the new institute will be to accelerate innovation and scaling up.
The government plans to strengthen protections against unwanted takeovers and investments in strategically important Dutch defense companies, as well as against leaks of sensitive technology and expertise, with a target to have additional legal instruments in place from 2028.

Federal prosecutors charged 14 people in an alleged $22.5 million cargo theft conspiracy targeting freight trains across Southern California. Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, allegedly coordinated burglaries involving more than 70 shipping containers. The operation targeted Nike sneakers, Milwaukee tools, JBL electronics and other consumer products. Investigators traced shipments from railroad tracks to residential storage locations and commercial resale businesses.
The defendants allegedly cut train air hoses to trigger emergency stops before removing valuable freight. Accomplices drove trucks and vans to predetermined locations, collected merchandise and transported it to nearby residences. Other participants inventoried products, negotiated prices and arranged deliveries to buyers. Prosecutors describe train burglaries spanning February 2024 through August 2026.
A 49-page federal indictment, filed Nov. 12, details 122 overt acts connected to the operation. Charges include conspiracy, interstate railroad cargo theft, receiving stolen freight and violence against railroad carriers. Investigators identified Union Pacific and BNSF trains among the targets. Many shipments originated through the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach.
The containers carried products destined for retailers and distribution centers across several states. Court records identify Indiana, Kansas, Texas and Pennsylvania among the intended destinations. Investigators obtained electronic communications, financial transactions and photographs documenting individual incidents. Those materials form much of the government’s case against the defendants.
How crews forced freight trains to stop
According to prosecutors, Angel coordinated participants who identified valuable shipments and selected locations along railroad tracks. Some suspects boarded trains while others operated vehicles or monitored surrounding areas. Donta Hedgeman allegedly helped disable equipment by cutting air hoses . The resulting pressure loss activated emergency brakes, allowing accomplices to remove cargo.
Federal investigators describe a March 11, 2025, burglary near Fullerton, California. Hedgeman texted Angel, “Where should I stop it,” at approximately 1:58 a.m. Angel responded four minutes later with a precise location along the tracks. Prosecutors accuse the crew of stealing Nike Air Max 270 sneakers during that operation.
Another exchange occurred July 29, 2025, during a theft involving JBL electronics. Hedgeman asked Angel, “Where u want me to cut it,” according to court records. Angel responded with an Apple Maps location near railroad tracks. Investigators estimate the missing products carried a retail value of about $158,000.
The indictment also describes the potential dangers of deliberately activating emergency braking systems. Sudden stops can damage couplers, separate equipment or cause railcars to derail. Federal authorities charged several defendants with violence against railroad carriers. Those counts concern incidents involving Union Pacific equipment carrying railroad personnel.
The group continued targeting trains during the summer of 2026, according to investigators. On July 15, conspirators allegedly stopped a Union Pacific shipment carrying Nike Air Jordan sneakers. Authorities valued at least 1,541 missing pairs at $269,835. Additional burglaries followed July 29, Aug. 5 and Aug. 6.
During the Aug. 6 incident, participants allegedly targeted unreleased Nike Air Jordan 9 “Space Jam” sneakers. The filing describes an emergency stop around 2:40 a.m. Investigators estimate the footwear carried a value of $299,050. The crew subsequently loaded merchandise into a box truck.
More than $1 million flowed through a resale business
Investigators connected portions of the merchandise to an unnamed Los Angeles sneaker and streetwear business. The indictment identifies the operation only as “Company 1.” Fredy Marquina and Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez allegedly supplied thousands of stolen Nike sneakers and other products. Between May and October 2025, the business paid approximately $1,081,493 for those purchases.
Financial records describe cash payments, wire transfers and deliveries to a Santa Monica warehouse. Marquina allegedly negotiated transactions while Martinez received funds through banking channels. Ricardo Mares also participated in transporting merchandise to designated locations. Prosecutors contend the company subsequently resold the products for profit.
One transaction followed a July 2025 burglary involving unreleased Nike Air Force 1 sneakers. Marquina offered a company representative 600 pairs for $60 each. The buyer responded, “I’ll buy all air forces … Bring asap.” Court records describe subsequent cash and wire payments totaling $32,500 for those shoes and other merchandise.
Another sale occurred Oct. 1, 2025, after thieves targeted Nike Air Max 95 sneakers. Investigators estimate the missing shipment carried a retail value of $294,120. Marquina negotiated approximately 693 pairs for $80 each. The defendants delivered those products to the Santa Monica warehouse that afternoon.
A separate resale operation involved social media accounts and residential storage. Jorge Angel Aguilar Espinoza allegedly received footwear, electronics and Milwaukee apparel at his Los Angeles residence. Investigators documented factory cartons, cash and inventory photographs connected to those transactions. Prosecutors contend Espinoza advertised merchandise online before selling it for profit.
Photos from the federal indictment show boxes of Nike sneakers and other merchandise stored at locations tied to the alleged cargo theft ring. (Photos: U.S. DOJ)
Messages and photographs document the operation
Federal investigators obtained communications connecting defendants to individual burglaries and merchandise transactions. The indictment includes photographs allegedly captured during thefts in February and October 2024. One image shows a participant cutting a container lock aboard a moving train. Others depict valuable products, large cash bundles and storage locations.
A July 2026 Instagram conversation involved a group called “Los Trenes.” Participants shared images, shipment information and messages concerning railroad activity. On July 14, Angel posted, “We found shoes,” after reaching Union Pacific tracks. Another participant responded, “Whoop Jordan’s,” referencing Nike Air Jordan sneakers.
Images shared in the “Los Trenes” Instagram group chat, which federal prosecutors linked to the alleged $22.5 million freight train cargo theft conspiracy. (Photos: U.S. DOJ)
The following morning, prosecutors contend conspirators disabled a train and removed its cargo. Messages described the incident, including a participant writing, “Stopped it good.” Investigators also obtained video showing merchandise unloading at a storage location after another burglary. Court records identify several defendants through those communications.
Other exchanges show participants discussing tracking devices inside stolen shipments. In July 2025, Espinoza asked whether someone had checked merchandise boxes for trackers. An October message referenced a load containing such equipment. January 2026 communications also addressed arrests and missing inventory.
The 17-count indictment names Angel and 13 co-defendants across multiple criminal charges. Prosecutors seek forfeiture of proceeds traceable to the offenses if convictions occur. The indictment does not identify Company 1 by name or charge its representatives in this case. All defendants remain presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
Why it matters
The alleged scheme exposes how organized criminals can turn moving freight trains into targets without accessing traditional cargo facilities. Cutting air hoses creates derailment risks, threatens railroad workers and disrupts shipments moving across the country. The resale network also shows how stolen freight can reach commercial markets long after thieves leave the tracks.

Here's What It Takes On Average To Ship a 13-Foot Camper to the US From Around the World
9 photos
Photo: Niewiadów
I was recently looking for some of the world’s lightest and most affordable campers, with Australia under the looking glass. It’s here that I ran across something that was to be expected: a brand selling a camper that’s designed, built, and used heavily on another continent.
Seeing campers being sold overseas in nations where they didn’t see their birth is nothing new, but what most people don’t understand is that, to sell a camper outside of the country where it was initially conceived comes with some drawbacks, one of the primary being that cost is almost always higher than if they were being sold on their maternal grounds.
Photo: Niewiadów As mentioned, all this started off with the camper before use, which in Australia is marketed and sold as the Euro Glider but which is in fact a variation of a Niewiadów N126, a camper which, on its native continent, sells for around €8,500, or roughly US$9,400. This means around AU$14,000, all this at exchange rates at the time of publishing.
However, the N126 series is currently up for grabs at around AU$36,000 through some dealers in Australia, so over double the price of the initial unit. Sure, some profit for the team selling it is to be accounted for, and some upgrades, although the unit does come across as one of the most basic out there, leaving us with a rather high “premium.”
Jumps in prices are primarily the result of one very important stage in bringing an import to your doorstep, just that, bringing it over to you, which means “ delivery fees .” You have to be unaware of how the world works to think that you can just bring an RV over to the US from another country and not have to pay a premium for it.
Photo: Niewiadów That said, I’ve decided to do a bit of research and find out what it can cost you to bring a simple travel trailer over to the US from various continents, so that you can have an idea of what to expect if you ever run into an import RV and want to make it your own but it isn’t already sold locally.
To make things easier to understand, we can continue to have the Niewiadów N126 in the spotlight, a camper born over in Poland. It’s comes in with a GVWR of 750 kg (1,653 lbs), occupies a space that’s almost 4 m (13 ft) long, 2 m (6.5 ft) wide, and 2,2 m (7.3 ft) tall.
According to sources, it’ll depend a whole lot on the method of shipping and the size of the package. Since we already know the dimensions, we can start with FCL of container shipping. For a 20-ft container (smallest option), we need on average of $4,500 to get things rolling right out of Poland.
Photo: Ian Taylor If you’re looking for a cheaper route, you can opt for a Roll-on and Roll-off (Ro-Ro) method which may save you around $1,500 but stores the camper below deck and exposes it to rough port handling. The issue here is that you will need to make sure the camper leaves from a port that can handle this method, and for the N126, you have to head over to Germany to do so.
This means extra cash dropped on getting the camper there in the first place, so you might as well opt for container shipping anyway.
Now there are several countries that produce campers which Americans are sure to want to get their hands on, and so so, I’ve put together a list of nations from where we can import a Niewiadów N126-sized camper. Keep in mind that these are averages and shipping rates do differ from one company to the next.
Australia FCL: $4,800 Ro-Ro: $3,000 China FCL: $4,500 Ro-Ro: $5,000 South Africa FCL: $2,500 Ro-Ro: $2,500 India FCL: $3,500 Ro-Ro: $3,500 Italy FCL: $3,500 Ro-Ro: $2,500 Germany 20FCL: $3,500 Ro-Ro: $3,500 UK FCL: $2,500 Ro-Ro: $2,000
Now, these are just a couple nations that we can typically import from and again, just some averages that I scrounged up. Sometimes, prices do exceed what I’ve jotted down and sometimes, even fall below those numbers.
Some of the countries on our list here are also nations from which American dealers already import campers or the brands themselves are selling units on US soil. Australia is one of them and so is Italy. China also makes the list, but they make the list for just about any nation in the world and quite heavily in Australia.
Photo: Ali Mkumbwa If you find an Australian, Italian, Chinese, or camper from any other nation other than the US, you understand why the usual premium pricing.
However, this is not all importing a camper entails, with fees like port handling falling into the bill you’ll need to cover, along with customs fees, DOT fees, some of which can will blow your mind, and again, the size of the unit you’re shipping will greatly impact how much you pay for one. Fees, fees, fees.
That said, while our example of the Niewiadów N126 being sold in Australia at over double it’s price may sound farfetched, this little example of what it can take to import a unit should tell you a bit about why we’re always paying extra for imported goods, not just campers. Then there’s Trump, but that’s a story for another day.
PS Keep in mind that these rates apply to campers that fit in a 20-foot container and sources mention that shipping companies calculate rates based on volume and weight and bill you for whichever results in the highest price for the service.

By Alison Koo
20 November 2026
Worsening bottlenecks in South-east Asian ports have resulted in intra-Asia rates moving up, even as congestion in China eases.
Yesterday, Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI) edged up $4 from 12 November, to $1,444 per 40ft, Shanghai-Manila rates rose 7%, to $1,310 per 40ft, while Shanghai-Laem Chabang increased 2%. to $1,584 per 40ft.
But average vessel waiting times on the two routes increased four hours and two hours, respectively.
Congestion intensified at major transhipment hubs, particularly Singapore, pushing rates from Shanghai to the port up 1%, to $2,064 per 40ft.
The Loadstar’s checks with Chinese ecommerce platform Pinduoduo showed customers had been advised to expect delays of around a week, due to vessel bunching around Singapore – Pinduoduo’s app noted: “Due to several ships docking in Singapore simultaneously, there have also been delays in unloading cargo.”
The easing of logjams in Chinese ports was reflected in the decline in intra-North Asia rates. Shanghai-Busan prices fell 8%, to $990 per 40ft, while Shanghai-Kaohsiung rates fell 3%, to $1,257 per 40ft, as average vessel waiting times decreased by three hours at Busan and four hours at Kaohsiung.
Ahead of the peak season for intra-Asia shipping, carriers have been deploying more capacity. Ferry operator Panstar Line, which piloted a Busan-Europe service through the Northern Sea Route in August, is starting a Busan-Incheon-Shekou-Hai Phong routing with compatriot feeder operator Pan-Continental Line next month.
